newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany fears French left win could soften euro.
newsitem.headline: Germany fears French left win could soften euro.

text.p: German economists said on Monday that a left-wing victory in France's run-off election next weekend could prompt Paris to seek softer membership criteria for the single European currency, German economists said on Monday.

A swing to the left in round one of France's parliamentary election on Sunday has raised the possibility that conservative President Jacques Chirac may be forced to share power with a left-wing government after the June 1 runoff.

Prospects for a government under Socialist leader Lionel Jospin prompted some economists to predict that Paris would not adopt strict German standards in interpreting the Maastricht Treaty and its guidelines for the new currency.
Some economists also said that a delay in currency union, set to begin in January 1999, would likely be discussed if the left wins a run-off election scheduled for next Sunday.

"If Britain is prepared to play with the thought of joining currency union in January 2002, then one could agree politically on that timing for the start date if a Socialist-led France does not meet the Maastricht Treaty criteria this year," said SGZ chief economist Frank Levin.

With most votes counted, the French interior ministry said on Monday the Socialists, Communists and other left had polled 40.23 percent and the ruling RPR-UDF coalition and other right-wing candidates 36.51 percent. The far-right National Front scored 14.90 percent and ecologists scored 6.81 percent.

Economists said the surprising strength of the left-wing, along with the prospect of the National Front seeking to play a kingmaker role, would dampen "euro euphoria" in France and Bonn would lose support in pushing for the euro's acceptance.

They also said a left-wing government may push for the deficit criteria set at 3.0 percent in the Maastricht Treaty to be raised to 3.2 percent of Gross Domestic Product -- a troubling hurdle for France as well as Germany.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin made clear in the run-up to the French election that he favoured a more flexible view of the Maastricht criteria, which lays out rules on deficit, debt and interest rate levels as well as foreign exchange rates.

Jospin has also voiced his dissatisfaction at Bonn, saying there was no reason why he should feel committed to a stability pact pushed by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel -- and agreed to by European Union nations, including France -- on deficit control after the launch of European monetary union.

Economists noted Jospin may view Germany's controversial plan to revalue the Bundesbank's gold reserves at market prices to help cut public debt as reason enough to seek his own interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty.

"If you take the gold valuation plans of the German government into account as well, then that's another sign that we are following the soft road to the euro," said Hermann Remsberger, chief economist at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.

Remsberger said a power change in France would also likely lead to a discussion over the independence of the European central bank, which will be based in Frankfurt and has been given broad independence from political meddling.
Jospin has pushed for the power of the future central bank to be weakened in favour of more power for politicians.
Jospin, who has promised to create hundreds of thousands of new jobs, made clear in election fight his party would not approve of any further cost-cutting measures to join the euro.
"That is certainly an argument against budget cuts," said economist Ulrike Kastens at Duesseldorf-based Trinkaus Capital Management of Jospin's job-growth plans.
